fix(release): verify no older tag survived the prune instead of assuming it

The prune ran gh release delete and git push --delete with every result discarded,
then printed released regardless — so a tag that failed to delete stayed on the
remote while the run reported success and the single-release policy quietly stopped
holding. A tag with no release makes the delete fail for a reason that is not a
problem, so no single call can judge itself: the remote is asked again afterwards
and a survivor fails the run.

fix(ci): give each prune run its own list, and stop reporting ok when it pruned nothing

Every managed repo prunes on the same self-hosted runner, and the run list was written to one
fixed path — two jobs overlapping meant the second overwrote the first's list, so the first then
asked its own repo to delete another repo's run ids. Every call 404s, the failure was swallowed,
and it printed ok having pruned nothing; the history kept growing with the job green. Proven:
with the fixed path a concurrent pair reads back each other's list, with a run-owned file it
does not.

A run already gone is still nothing to report, but anything else now names the run and fails,
so a systematic failure — a token without the scope — cannot look like a working prune.

fix(prune): a registry that will not answer is not a first publish, and a refused unpublish is not silence

npm exits non-zero both when a package has never been published and when the registry declines
to answer, so calling every failure 'first publish' turned an outage into a clean no-op that
skipped the prune entirely. Only a 404 means never-published now.

The unpublish results already recorded which versions npm refused, and only the successes were
printed — so a version that stayed on npm against the single-present-publish convention left no
trace, with the run green and the failure computed and dropped. Those versions are named now.

fix(release): a registry that will not answer is not 'nothing to publish'

npm exits non-zero both when a package is absent and when the registry declines to answer, so
resolving every failure to not-on-npm turned an outage into a clean 'no publishable package'
and exit 0 — a version bump would be dropped with the run green and no trace. Only a 404 means
absent now; anything else fails with the name that could not be resolved.

The tag and release were fire-and-forget after a successful publish, so the package could land
on npm with nothing pointing at it while the script still printed 'released'. The next run then
sees the version already published and never retries, so the gap is permanent and invisible.
It reports and exits non-zero instead.

test: run the e2e suite in CI — 59 tests had no gate, and one stale selector

Nothing has ever run these: no test script existed in this repo's history, so when the file
tree stopped being a <nav> (it is a div; the ref is still called navRef) the shared waitTree
helper's selector matched nothing and no gate noticed. Selecting on the label instead of the
element name survives markup that keeps the same semantics — all 59 pass.

The config also pinned port 3001 with reuse enabled, and this machine serves another project
there: any run would have adopted that server and tested someone else's app. The port is now
allocated once by scripts/e2e.sh and exported — playwright re-evaluates its config in every
worker, so a port computed inside it differs per worker while only the webServer's answers —
and reuse is off so a stray process fails the run instead of hijacking it.

Verified through the wired path: @idecn/web:test reports 59 passed.

fix(registry): gate the registry from this repo's action, not the fleet-managed up.sh

up.sh is shared across every managed repo and only this one ships a registry, so the check
lives beside what it guards and hangs off action, which CI already runs. Same two halves,
both still proven: the generator refuses an unbuildable item, and this refuses a committed

fix(registry): make the generator refuse a broken registry, and gate it on every run

The defects this artifact shipped were each invisible in the JSON and only surfaced in a
consumer's build, so the generator now asserts what it emits: no workspace-private import
survives a rewrite, every alias resolves to an emitted file or a declared registryDependency,
and every npm import is declared by some manifest. Proven against a planted regression — the
single-quote rewrite that caused the original leak now exits non-zero and names the files.

The check ran only when someone remembered to call it, which is why none of this was caught;
up.sh regenerates and diffs the committed copy on every run, so a stale registry or an
unbuildable one fails there instead of in someone else's app.

fix(registry): ship a registry a consumer can actually build

The published item resolved only inside this monorepo: every emitted file kept its
workspace-private @a/ui imports (the rewrite matched one quote style, and the vendored
files use the other), scoped packages never reached the dependency list (the extraction
regex excluded @), a sibling module the component imports was never emitted, and the
vendored files' own deps were invisible to a scan of the main component. Each is derived
from what is emitted now, so a new import cannot silently miss the manifest.

The registry test that would have caught this could not run: it fed a workspace: dep to
bun add, piped the build through tail so the failing module names were discarded, and the
add stopped on an overwrite prompt a non-tty answered No — so the components never landed
and the build failed on files the add was meant to write. It also raced any other run on
this machine through a fixed port and the shared .next.

A consumer's scaffold targets ES2017, where the component's one named capture group is a
type error; a replacer over the whole match splits camelCase identically with no groups.
